title: Simulation Task
description: Develop a multi-agent simulation system that models the spread of mask-wearing behavior through social networks.
simulation_focus: Predict agents' mask-wearing behavior over day 30 - day 39 (last ten days) based on their attributes, social connections, and past behavior
Model information propagation and behavioral changes triggered by social influence and government intervention starting on Day 10

data_files.agent_attributes.csv: Contains demographic and behavioral attributes of each agent, including age, occupation, risk perception, and social connection counts
data_files.social_network.json: Contains structured data representing a social network. Each entry corresponds to a user (identified by a unique integer ID), and the values describe the different types of relationships that user has with others. Data Structure: The top-level structure is a dictionary ({} in JSON). Keys: Each key is a unique user ID (as an integer, e.g., 0, 1, 2, etc.). Values: Each value is another dictionary with the following fields: "family": a list of user IDs representing family connections. "work_school": a list of user IDs representing colleagues or schoolmates. "community": a list of user IDs representing community-level acquaintances. "all": a merged list of all user IDs connected to the user across the three categories above.
data_files.train_data.csv: Time series data for the first 30 days, used for training the model

RMSE.description: Root Mean Square Error measuring overall predictive accuracy of mask adoption rates
RMSE.interpretation: Directly interpretable as percentage deviations due to the 0-1 range

Peak Adoption Rate Error.description: Measures model accuracy in predicting maximum mask adoption during intervention

Time-to-Peak Error.description: Measures model accuracy in predicting the time lag from intervention to peak behavior change

key_patterns.name: Multiplex network with distinct layers
key_patterns.description: Agents have separate connection counts in family, work/school, and community layers with total_connections equal to the sum. Family ties are few but tight, work/school moderate, and community broader.
key_patterns.relevance: Layer-specific influence strengths and contact rates should differ; calibration should preserve per-layer degree targets and clustering (especially in family).

key_patterns.name: Risk-perception-driven baseline adoption
key_patterns.description: Risk_perception (0–1) is an intrinsic propensity likely positively associated with initial_mask_wearing and subsequent adoption without social cues.
key_patterns.relevance: Supports a baseline adoption hazard or threshold offset per agent proportional to risk_perception.

key_patterns.name: Heterogeneity by age_group and occupation
key_patterns.description: Age_group and occupation segment contact patterns and susceptibility/influence. Expect homophily (same age_group/occupation more likely connected) and different responsiveness (e.g., students in work/school layer).
key_patterns.relevance: Calibrate layer-specific homophily and group-specific influence or thresholds to reproduce differential uptake.

key_patterns.name: Information exposure boosts adoption
key_patterns.description: Panel data includes received_info; adoption events tend to follow days with received_info.
key_patterns.relevance: Calibrate exogenous information effect and/or use it to infer peer-driven information processes in-network.

key_patterns.name: State persistence with occasional abandonment
key_patterns.description: Wearing_mask is sticky day-to-day with some abandonment probability, likely lower than adoption probability when peers/info are present.
key_patterns.relevance: Include both adoption and abandonment processes with different determinants and rates.

key_distributions.name: Per-layer degree distributions
key_distributions.description: Family, work_school, and community degrees per agent are overdispersed relative to Poisson (typical for social networks).
key_distributions.parameters: Fit Negative Binomial for each layer: mean (mu_family, mu_work, mu_comm) and dispersion (k_family, k_work, k_comm); verify total_connections ≈ sum.

key_distributions.name: Risk perception distribution
key_distributions.description: risk_perception spans 0–1; often unimodal with skew depending on population.
key_distributions.parameters: Fit Beta(a_risk, b_risk) to risk_perception; also compute quantiles per age_group and occupation.

key_distributions.name: Initial mask adoption prevalence
key_distributions.description: Share of agents with initial_mask_wearing = true at t0.
key_distributions.parameters: p_init = mean(initial_mask_wearing); segment by age_group and occupation for priors.

key_distributions.name: Layer-specific masked-neighbor exposure
key_distributions.description: Distribution of fraction of masked neighbors per layer over time (from panel + network).
key_distributions.parameters: Empirical distribution of f_family, f_work, f_comm; use to calibrate influence response curves.

key_distributions.name: Adoption and abandonment hazards
key_distributions.description: Discrete-time transition probabilities conditional on prior state and received_info.
key_distributions.parameters: p_adopt0 = P(wear_t=1 | wear_{t-1}=0, info=0); p_adopt1 = P(..., info=1); p_drop0 = P(wear_t=0 | wear_{t-1}=1, info=0); p_drop1 = P(..., info=1).

key_relationships.relationship: Positive association; higher risk_perception corresponds to higher initial adoption probability.
key_relationships.strength: To quantify via logistic regression; expected moderate.

key_relationships.relationship: Strong positive effect of received information on same-day or next-day adoption among non-wearers.
key_relationships.strength: Expected strong; estimate odds ratio from panel.

key_relationships.relationship: Higher layer-specific masked-neighbor fraction increases adoption probability; family expected strongest marginal effect.
key_relationships.strength: Calibrate layer coefficients; family > work/school > community.

key_relationships.relationship: Homophily: ties more likely between agents with the same occupation category in work/school.
key_relationships.strength: Estimate assortativity coefficient; expected moderate to high.

key_relationships.relationship: Baseline adoption and abandonment differ by age_group; younger groups may respond more to work/school peers.
key_relationships.strength: Estimate group fixed effects; expected small to moderate.

layer_degree_targets.value: Use per-agent family_connections, work_school_connections, community_connections; validate total_connections consistency.
layer_degree_targets.notes: Generate edges via configuration model per layer with constraints; cap to available stubs and avoid self/multi-edges when possible.

edge_symmetry.value: Symmetrize adjacency lists; treat edges as undirected.
edge_symmetry.notes: If an edge appears in one direction, add reciprocal; remove self-loops; deduplicate.

family_clustering_target.source: Derived from typical household clustering; refine using triangle counts in family layer from JSON if present
family_clustering_target.notes: Use triadic closure probability during generation to reach target clustering; calibrate to observed clustering if measurable.

homophily_coefficients.source: Estimate from mixing matrices between attributes and edges (JSON) or from degree targets by segment
homophily_coefficients.notes: Used as preference weights in edge formation; higher values enforce more within-group ties.

layer_influence_weights.source: To be calibrated from panel by regressing adoption on layer-specific exposure; prior based on social proximity
layer_influence_weights.notes: Weights should sum to 1; adjust to best fit adoption dynamics.

baseline_adoption_scale_alpha.source: Panel calibration; prior for mapping risk_perception to daily adoption hazard: p_base = alpha * risk_perception
baseline_adoption_scale_alpha.notes: Ensure p_base ∈ [0,1]; cap if necessary; can alternatively calibrate as intercept in logistic model.

social_influence_coefficient.source: Panel: logistic regression coefficient on weighted masked-neighbor fraction
social_influence_coefficient.notes: In a logit: logit(p_adopt) = ... + beta * exposure; initial beta prior ~ 1–3; calibrate.

abandonment_base_prob.source: Panel: P(wear_t=0 | wear_{t-1}=1, exposure low, info=0)
abandonment_base_prob.notes: Allow abandonment to decrease with higher exposure; e.g., p_drop = p0 * exp(-gamma * exposure).

exposure_effect_by_layer.source: Panel calibration of marginal effects; prior emphasizes family influence
exposure_effect_by_layer.notes: These multiply the neighbor masked fraction before aggregation.

threshold_distribution.source: Alternative to logistic contagion; infer from observed exposure at adoption events
threshold_distribution.notes: If using threshold model, each agent draws a threshold; risk_perception can shift the threshold.

exogenous_info_schedule.value: Replay received_info per agent-day; or fit a model linking peer masks to probability of info receipt.
exogenous_info_schedule.notes: If not replaying, model P(info_t=1) as function of neighbor masks and broadcast campaigns.

info_to_adoption_effect.source: Panel: compare adoption odds with vs without received_info among non-wearers
info_to_adoption_effect.notes: Implement as additive logit term or as multiplicative hazard scaler.

initial_mask_seed.notes: Cross-check with panel day 0; resolve conflicts by trusting panel if available.

time_horizon_and_step.value: Daily time steps; horizon = max(day) in panel

tracked_outputs.source: Derived for validation against panel aggregates
tracked_outputs.notes: Compute same aggregates on panel for direct comparison.

preprocessing_steps.purpose: Convert booleans to binary, check non-negativity of degrees, verify total_connections equals sum of layer degrees.
From social_network.json, deduplicate neighbors, remove self-edges, symmetrize; else generate per-layer edges to match degree sequences with homophily and clustering.
Attach age_group, occupation, risk_perception, initial state to nodes for homophily and influence modeling.
Create lagged wearing_mask_{t-1}, compute per-layer masked neighbor fractions at t-1, align received_info by day; handle missing days by forward-fill or explicit gaps.
Split by train/validation time windows and by demographic segments for robust estimation and validation.

calibration_strategy.calibration_approach: Two-stage calibration. Stage 1 (network): Fit per-layer degree distributions and mixing patterns. If JSON network is provided, compute empirical stats (degree distributions, clustering, assortativity) and use them directly or to tune the synthetic generator (configuration model with homophily and triadic closure). Stage 2 (behavior): Estimate discrete-time event models on the panel. For adoption (among non-wearers), fit a logistic regression or complementary log-log hazard: wear_t ~ risk_perception + weighted masked exposure by layer + received_info + age_group + occupation + interactions. For abandonment (among wearers), fit analogous model with exposure expected to reduce dropping. Map estimated coefficients to simulation parameters: intercepts to baseline hazards, layer coefficients to influence weights, group fixed effects to group-specific offsets, and info coefficient to exogenous boost. Optionally estimate an individual random effect to capture unobserved heterogeneity; approximate in simulation via per-agent noise or threshold draws.
calibration_strategy.validation_strategy: Out-of-sample and multi-level validation. 1) Hold-out final K days to test predictive prevalence curves (RMSE/MAE) and event-rate calibration (Brier score). 2) Cross-sectional validation: compare adoption prevalence by age_group and occupation over time. 3) Network-level validation: reproduce exposure-response curves (adoption probability vs masked-neighbor fraction by layer). 4) Structural validation: if generating a network, compare degree distributions (KS test), clustering, and assortativity to targets. 5) Sensitivity analysis: vary key parameters (layer weights, abandonment base) within confidence intervals and check robustness of diffusion trajectories.

file_summaries:
- Overall data structure and type
  - Flat CSV; one row per agent (node). Columns are a mix of integer, float, boolean, and categorical fields. No nested structures or explicit edge lists.

- Meaning of keys or columns
  - agent_id: Unique node identifier; primary key for agents.
  - age (int), age_group (categorical): Individual demographic; age_group is a derived bucket from age (redundant but useful for grouping/homophily).
  - occupation (categorical): Role category (e.g., Student, Blue/White Collar); can inform contact patterns in the work/school layer.
  - risk_perception (float 0–1): Intrinsic propensity to adopt mask-wearing; candidate for baseline adoption probability or threshold parameter.
  - initial_mask_wearing (bool): Seed adoption state at t0.
  - family_connections, work_school_connections, community_connections (ints): Desired degree per agent in each network layer.
  - total_connections (int): Sum of the three layer degrees; redundant consistency check.

- Relationships or nested elements
  - Implicit multiplex network: three layers (family, work/school, community). The file provides per-agent degree targets per layer but no explicit ties; total_connections = family + work/school + community.
  - No household IDs or group memberships are given; “family_connections” indicates degree, not membership.

- How this data should inform simulation entities or interactions
  - Agents: Create one agent per row with attributes (age, age_group, occupation, risk_perception, initial_mask_wearing).
  - Network generation: For each layer, synthesize edges to match the provided degree sequence (e.g., configuration model), optionally adding homophily by age_group/occupation and clustering for family. Use total_connections for validation.
  - Dynamics: Initialize mask state from initial_mask_wearing. Model adoption probability as a function of:
    - Personal factor: risk_perception (e.g., baseline hazard or threshold).
    - Social influence: fraction/number of masked neighbors per layer, with optional layer weights (e.g., family > work/school > community).
    - Demographic/occupation modifiers if desired (e.g., students more influenced in school layer).
  - Measurement: Track diffusion over time by layer and demographic segments; use degrees to compute exposure and influence centrality.

Semantic metadata summary for social_network.json

- Overall structure and type:
  - JSON object representing a multilayer social network as adjacency lists.
  - Top-level keys are agent IDs (strings of integers, e.g., "0", "1", ...), likely spanning 0–999 (1000 agents, inferred from IDs like 998/999).

- Meaning of keys/columns:
  - Each agent maps to an object with four keys:
    - family: list of agent IDs connected via household/family ties.
    - work_school: list of agent IDs connected via workplace/school ties.
    - community: list of agent IDs connected via general community ties (neighborhood, social clubs, etc.).
    - all: union of the above three lists for that agent (intended aggregate neighborhood).

- Relationships and nesting:
  - Nested lists are adjacency lists (neighbors) per social context (layer).
  - The network is multiplex/multilayer: family, work_school, and community are distinct layers.
  - The all list aggregates neighbors across layers; duplicates appear to be removed (union), but do not assume ordering.
  - Edges may not be symmetric in the raw data (i.e., directed vs. undirected unspecified). No self-edges shown in sample.

- How to use this data in the simulation:
  - Agents: each top-level key defines one agent node.
  - Layers: implement three influence layers with potentially different interaction frequencies/weights (e.g., strongest in family, moderate in work/school, weakest in community).
  - Edges/interactions:
    - For each agent, contacts are the IDs in the respective lists; use all for general interactions or select by layer for time-of-day or context-specific scheduling.
    - If the model assumes undirected ties, symmetrize adjacency (add missing reciprocals) during preprocessing.
    - Treat lists as sets (deduplicate) and exclude self-edges if any appear.
  - Initialization and dynamics:
    - Use degree in each layer to set exposure opportunities; allow layer-specific adoption probabilities or thresholds.
    - Optionally weight edges by layer when computing social influence toward mask adoption.
    - The all list can speed up global neighborhood queries; layer lists enable differential policies (e.g., work mandates vs. community norms).

Notes:
- Validate global node set and ID range; confirm that all neighbor IDs exist as keys.
- Consider constructing a multiplex graph (e.g., NetworkX with edge attribute layer) or three layer-specific graphs plus an aggregate.

- Data type and structure: CSV, flat rectangular panel (longitudinal) format. Each row is one agent-day observation. Primary key is composite (agent_id, day).
- Columns and meanings:
  - day (int): Discrete time step (appears 0-indexed); implies daily synchronous updates.
  - agent_id (int): Unique agent identifier; groups rows into individual time series.
  - wearing_mask (bool): Agent’s behavioral state on that day (1 = wearing, 0 = not).
  - received_info (bool): Whether the agent received pro-mask information on that day (exogenous or via social contacts).
- Relationships/nesting:
  - No nested elements; repeated rows per agent form sequences over time.
  - No network topology or inter-agent edges provided; cross-agent relationships are not encoded here.
  - Temporal dependency implied: wearing_mask(t) depends on prior state and possibly received_info(t) (and peers, if supplied elsewhere).
- How to use in the simulation:
  - Agent state variables: wearing_mask (state), received_info (event/input).
  - Initialization: Use day 0 records to set initial wearing_mask; optionally seed initial info events from received_info at day 0.
  - Calibration: Estimate transition probabilities P(wearing_mask_t | wearing_mask_{t-1}, received_info_t) and spontaneous adoption/abandonment rates when received_info = false.
  - Exogenous inputs: Use received_info as a scheduled external stimulus, or as labels to learn how network-driven info should be generated in the model.
  - Network layer: Provide or learn a separate graph (not in this file) to propagate information; couple peer influence to probability of received_info and/or direct social contagion of wearing_mask.
  - Update scheme: Synchronous daily updates to match data granularity; include lagged features (previous day’s state).
  - Parsing notes: Booleans in CSV likely as “true/false” strings; convert to binary. Handle missing days per agent by forward-fill or explicit “no data” rules if encountered.
